title: Consultancy to Develop Learning Paper 2 for SPREAD- Integrating Peacebuilding, Livelihoods, Climate Resilience and Disaster Risk Reduction
draft_excerpt:
## ORGANISATIONAL PROFILE

Cortech Consulting Group is an international development consulting firm founded in 2015, with registered offices in Nairobi (Kenya), Mogadishu (Somalia) and London (United Kingdom).
The firm is a registered company in Kenya, licensed to operate in Somalia, and a registered company in the United Kingdom; Cortech is ISO certified and maintains child safeguarding and PSEA policies in force.
Cortech's primary geographic focus is Somalia, Kenya and Ethiopia, with secondary presence extending to Sudan, South Sudan, Uganda, Tanzania, Malawi and Djibouti, giving the firm continuous operational reach across all three SPREAD countries: Kenya, Ethiopia and South Sudan.
Cortech's core thematic areas include Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning; Research, Assessment and Documentation; Community Engagement and Participatory Research; Urban Resilience and Climate Adaptation; Refugee/Displacement and Protection Programming; Livelihoods and Economic Inclusion; and Policy Analysis and Advocacy, which together span the peacebuilding, livelihoods, climate resilience and Disaster Risk Reduction components this assignment requires DCA to examine as an integrated whole rather than as siloed sectors.
The firm's tools and methodologies include KoboToolbox, SPSS, NVivo, Python/R, QGIS, OECD DAC evaluation criteria and Participatory Action Research, supporting the mixed-methods design (KIIs, FGDs, participatory ranking, data triangulation, disaggregation by sex, age and disability) that the SPREAD ToR specifies.
Cortech has worked with the Danish Refugee Council, IGAD, CEWARN, UNDP, UNICEF, Save the Children Somalia Country Office and other institutional clients on assignments spanning conflict-affected borderland settings, refugee and IDP contexts, and multi-sector nexus programming.
This places the firm directly against the requirement, stated in the ToR's Expected Qualifications, for "demonstrated experience in conducting research and learning assignments involving complex multi-sector programming, with the ability to assess linkages and synergies across peacebuilding, livelihoods, climate resilience and DRR interventions." Cortech's bilingual team (English, Somali, Swahili, with Arabic and French capacity) and rapid mobilisation model support fieldwork across dispersed, cross-border sites of the kind SPREAD requires in South Omo/Ethiopia, Turkana/Kenya and Eastern Equatoria/South Sudan.
Cortech's distinguishing position for this assignment is the combination of prior IGAD-facing regional policy work, prior climate-resilience-and-peacebuilding nexus evaluation, and continuous East African field presence, rather than any single credential in isolation.

Understanding of the Terms of Reference

DanChurchAid Kenya has commissioned this assignment as the second in a series of learning papers under the European Union-funded SPREAD programme ("Strengthening Integrated Peace, Resilience and Disaster Risk Reduction for Cross-border Communities"), implemented by DCA in partnership with TUPADO (Kenya), ROG and ICPDO (South Sudan), and ECC (Ethiopia) across the border regions of South Omo/Ethiopia, Turkana/Kenya and Eastern Equatoria/South Sudan [NOT VERIFIED]. SPREAD is now 42 months in duration and in its third, concluding year. Cortech understands that this Learning Paper 2 is not a conventional evaluation of activity delivery but a targeted, evidence-generating exercise that must answer a narrower and more difficult question than "did SPREAD work": what did integration actually mean operationally when peacebuilding, livelihoods, climate resilience and Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) components were delivered as one package rather than as parallel, siloed activities, and when did that integration add value beyond the sum of its parts. This distinction, explicit in the ToR's framing of SPREAD as "designed as an integrated programme," is the organising problem of the assignment and will organise our methodology, our sampling and our reporting. We understand that DCA already holds a body of experience on this question, generated through a dedicated reflection workshop conducted at Year 3/Mid-Term Review stage, and that this learning paper's task is to critically examine, document and extend that experience into actionable guidance rather than to re-discover it from a blank page [NOT VERIFIED]. Our desk review will therefore treat the SPREAD baseline report (2024), the Mid-Term Review report (2025) and the Year 3/MTR reflection workshop outputs as primary evidentiary inputs, alongside DCA's Conflict Prevention Action Guide 2024, Social Cohesion Action Guide 2024, the Social Cohesion Index tool, DCA's resilience-building framework, and DCA's guidance on Market Systems Development and Financial Inclusion. We also understand that the consultant is expected to build on SPREAD's existing Outcome Harvesting practice rather than substitute it with a generic qualitative method, and our data collection instruments will be designed explicitly to complement, not duplicate, the reflection workshop's findings. We read the assignment as requiring evidence against six specific objectives, and our proposed research questions and tools map directly to each:

1. Establishing, within the assignment period, a shared operational definition of integration as applied in SPREAD design and inception, documenting how sequencing and coordination between peacebuilding, livelihoods, climate resilience and DRR components were implemented in practice. We understand this requires distinguishing sequencing logics (for example, peace preceding livelihood investment, economic cooperation opening space for dialogue, or natural-resource agreements preceding irrigation or agricultural investment) rather than treating integration as a single undifferentiated concept. 2. Documenting the challenges and trade-offs of integrating different thematic activities at local level, including tensions between livelihoods and climate resilience/adaptation, and linking this explicitly to the broader agenda of reducing pressure on natural resources through diversified income opportunities. 3. Using community case studies, including both stronger and weaker examples of integration, to show how interventions were experienced as one package by communities and to explain why integrated programming worked better in some locations than others, drawing on direct engagement with community members, leaders and local authorities to capture their preferences for greater integration of community groups working on conflict prevention and DRR. 4. Assessing how communities relate to SPREAD-introduced structures, namely Community Action Groups (CAGs), Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLAs), micro-grants and early warning systems, alongside pre-existing structures such as market committees and savings groups, and capturing community, leader and local authority preferences for future integration. 5. Producing a detailed learning paper and a concise policy brief for donors, IGAD and governments, with SMART, evidence-based recommendations on which components should be integrated, at what level, and which can simply be coordinated, to inform future funding and programming models. 6. Developing a distinct, focused policy brief examining how SPREAD's integrated peacebuilding, livelihoods, climate resilience and DRR approach contributes to local and regional stability and human security, for policymakers

quality_score.weakest_criterion: Candidate's relevant academic qualifications for key experts (10%) — the draft names Mugove Kwashirai Chakurira and Akama Maiko Erick repeatedly but never states a single degree, qualification, or years of relevant academic training, leaving the assessor nothing to score against this weighted criterion.
quality_score.strongest_criterion: Have the Terms of Reference been addressed in sufficient detail (20%) — the understanding_of_the_terms_of_reference section names all six objectives, all six key learning questions verbatim, the exact deliverable dates (13 Oct, 21 Nov, 3 Dec, 15 Dec 2026), DCA's specific guidance documents (Conflict Prevention Action Guide, Social Cohesion Index), and the CMU/thematic-lead structure, none of which is generic and all of which is annex-level detail unique to this ToR.
quality_score.one_improvement: The key_research_questions section is not actually written — it stops after a truncated 'Introduction and Background' heading and never lists the six key learning questions, even though methodology_and_tools_to_be_used claims tools were 'built around the six proposed key learning questions verbatim'; this section must be completed with the full questions plus explicit sample-size figures per site/respondent group, since neither section currently states any numeric sample size despite the criterion explicitly asking whether 'sample size is adequate'.
